full_judgment:
6. Thereafter, the learned trial Court in consideration of the evidence on record as well as facts and circumstances of the case found the accused-appellant guilty for the offence-charged and, as such, convicted him thereunder and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life and also ordered to pay a fine of Taka 5,000 with default clause. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied thereby the accused as appellant has come up with the present appeal which is opposed by the respondent-State through the learned Deputy Attorney-General Md KM Saifuddin Ahmed. 

 7. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that this is a case of no evidence and the learned trial court failed to sift the evidence on record. He further submits that the learned trial Court failed to consider that there is no eye-witness to the occurrence and that the accused-appellant explained the death of the deceased. He lastly submits that the learned trial Court failed to consider the defence case and did not pay heed to the statement of the accused-appellant which he submitted and while examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and did not dispose of the petition for fresh post-mortem examination which has prejudiced the accused-appellant. Accordingly, he submits that the impugned judgment and order of conviction cannot be sustained. 

 17. PW 12 Md Shafiq Ullah, investigation officer of this case, proved the first information report and his signature thereto Exhibit 4, 4/1 respectively, the sketch-map with separate index of the place of occurrence along with his signature thereto Exhibits 5 & 6 series respectively. He claimed to have recorded the statement of witnesses under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and thereafter submitted a charge-sheet against the accused-appellant under section 302 of the Penal Code since prima facie case was made out against him. In cross, he admitted that during investigation he came to know that the accused filed an UD case over the occurrence wherein stated that the deceased was a cronic patient and that she committed suicide. He thereafter mentioned the names of owner of the house/room as shown in the sketch-map. He denied the defence suggestion that his inquiry was not proper and submitted an obliging charge-sheet. This is all about the evidence on record. 

 18. The critical analysis of the aforesaid evidence indicates that there is no eye-witness to the occurrence. However, there is no rule of law that if there be no eye-witness to a murder, the accused should not be sentenced to death. It is not difficult to procure false evidence of eye-witness. It is, on the other hand, extremely difficult to procure circumstantial evidence of a convincing character and therefore, circumstantial evidence, if convincing, is more cogent than the evidence of eye-witness. A finding of guilt against the accused cannot be based merely on the high probabilities. Court of law has to dispense justice in accordance with law and not according to the moral conviction of the judge with regard to the occurrence. A conviction on circumstantial evidence cannot be passed unless and until all the inferences to be drawn on the whole history of the case pointed so strongly to commission of crime by the accused that the defence version appears in the face of it impossible or highly improbable. Keeping in view of the aforesaid principle, let us now examine the evidence which was adduced by the prosecution. 

 19. In this case admittedly the private witnesses are close relations of the accused and some admitted neighbours who are public representatives as is evident from the sketch-map and index of the place of occurrence Exhibits 5 and 6 respectively. The private witnesses either relations of the accused or close neighbours who are public representatives too did not state about any ill-treatment of the accused-appellant with the deceased during her lifetime save and except PW 9 who happens to be the brother of the deceased. In this connection we must mention some unusual facts regarding the PW 9. PW 9 is admitted full-brother of the deceased and he categorically admitted that he came to know about serious illness of the deceased at 5-00 PM on the date (though there is nothing on record to show that accused ever took plea that the deceased was seriously ill and that he ever intimated anybody about this fact), but he did not turn up to see his sister in the said night. Further, it appears that on the following day he went straight to Thana where the dead body was waiting for transfer to morgue for holding post mortem examination. This PW 9 claimed that the relationship between the accused and the deceased was not good inasmuch as the accused use to ill-treat/beat the deceased off and on. But this fact appears to have got no corroboration of any independent witness. The contention of this PW, the brother of the deceased, who comes to see the dead body of the deceased at police station being aware about the seriousness of the deceased on the previous date, should be swallowed with a grain of salt. We have already mentioned earlier that all the private PWs except PW 9 categorically said that the deceased committed suicide and the informant of this case, who lodged suo moto first information report also admitted on dock that he heard at the time of preparation of inquest report on the dead body of the deceased that the latter committed suicide. It also appears from the evidence of private PWs that the son of the deceased, who happens to be a student of class-VI, allegedly reported that his mother committed suicide. It may be argued from the side of the respondent that this fact has not been corroborated by any tangible evidence on record, but fact remains that some of the private PWs have stated this fact on oath and that the defence failed to examine the son of the deceased in this case in order to show its bona fide. The presence of the son of the deceased as a witness was very much relevant in this case and non-examination of him very much tells upon the prosecution case and in such circumstances the benefit of section 114(g) of the Evidence Act must go to the defence. So, in absence of any -direct evidence that the accused had ever illtreated/beaten the deceased during her life time by any direct evidence in the face of cogent evidence on record by some of the private witnesses that the deceased committed suicide should not be ignored lightly. 

 21. In the instant case it appears that the inquest report bears the description of an injury on the forehead of the deceased as 'small', but the post-mortem examination report described the same injury measuring 3" x 2" x bone deep which, in no way, can be termed as 'small' and in view of such anomaly we are really in doubt about the measurement of the injury in question as found on the forehead of the deceased, specially in the face of failure to hold second post-mortem examination on the dead body of the deceased in spite of the prayer of the accused-appellant made immediately after receipt of the post-mortem examination report and this view has further been supported by the rulings in the case of Taleb alias Talabor Rahman and another vs State reported in PLD 1967 SC 16 = 19 DLR (SC) 134. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, however, referred to a decision in the case of Dipok Kumar Sarker vs State reported in 40 DLR (AD) 139 and submits that since the deceased, the wife of the accused, died in latter's residence, the husband is to prove otherwise and the accused having failed to discharge his duty as to how she met with death it is presumed that the accused murdered the deceased and, as such, he contends that the same justifies that the prosecution has successfully proved its case. The submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General appears to be conventional one, because the facts and circumstances of the present case in no way agree with the aforesaid reported case. Because, there is persistent evidence on record to show that the accused went to Thana and lodged GD entry informing the unnatural death of the deceased just immediately after the occurrence over which the UD case in question was started. Further, it appears that the informant himself admitted that the dead body of the deceased was identified by the accused and that the latter was all along present when he prepared the inquest inasmuch as he did not go else where till he was arrested by police after filing of suo moto first information report. The matter did not end there. The accused filed a petition before the Court below challenging the post mortem examination report of the deceased immediately after the receipt of the same/remaining in hajot, but the learned Court below failed to pass any order on the same. Coupled with this the learned trial Court found to have not considered the written statement so made by the accused-appellant during his examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure backed by several prescriptions and hospital papers starting from 1983. The close scrutiny of the prescription and hospital papers so filed by the accused-appellant during his examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure indicates that the deceased attempted twice to commit suicide and both the times she was saved due to timely intervention of the accused-appellant and there is nothing on record to show that those prescriptions and hospital papers are forged and back-dated inasmuch as the same had been prepared for the purpose of the case.
